title: Have you seen God?
hookLine: a skeptical student asks every teacher the same question, and one says yes
carry: the rishis saw, and so can you

lines: ONE QUESTION: HAVE YOU SEEN GOD?
cards: Calcutta, in the early 1880s. A college student named Narendranath Datta is sharp, restless and hard to impress. He goes from one religious teacher to another with a single blunt question: have you seen God?
He gets speeches, and arguments, and no straight answer. Then he meets a temple priest at Dakshineswar, Ramakrishna, and asks him too.

And Ramakrishna, by Narendra's own later account, says yes: he sees God the way he sees the young man in front of him, only more intensely. And, the early biographies add, he offers to show Narendra too.

teach.h: THE TEACHERS DIDN'T ONLY BELIEVE; THEY SAW.
teach.b: Years later, Vivekananda built a whole book on that answer. It's called Raja Yoga, the yoga of the mind, and it opens with an argument. The great teachers of religion, he says, did not only believe.
They saw. They spoke of what they had perceived for themselves. That's an old Hindu idea, not a new one.
The poets of the Vedas are called rishis, seers, and tradition says the Vedas weren't made up by them but seen and heard.
So, Vivekananda says, if one person has perceived something, others can perceive it too, given the right method. Religion, in his telling, shouldn't rest only on someone else's report.
It can be tested by experience. And Raja Yoga asks for no belief at the start. Try it, and see.
Then the twist. The lab isn't somewhere else.

teach.h: THE LAB IS THE MIND ITSELF.
teach.b: The instrument is the mind itself, and it doesn't hold still long enough to observe anything. So the book gets practical: posture, breath, learning to watch the mind.
Its second half carries his rendering of Patanjali's Yoga Sutras, which open: now, the teaching of yoga.
This is why many Hindu teachers speak of faith less as a list of opinions to sign and more as practice: the sit, the name, the prayer, done until you see for yourself.
So when someone asks, do you really believe all that, a Hindu can honestly say: my tradition invites me to look.

how: Vivekananda's Raja Yoga is read and studied in Ramakrishna Mission and Vedanta Society centers, often alongside Patanjali's Yoga Sutras, and students describe starting with posture, breath and watching the mind.

o: a creed to accept before any practice starts
a yoga of the mind, to be tested by experience
a set of court rules for kings and queens

games.q: have you seen God? — tap the pairs.
p: yes, and i can show you
seers: they saw what they taught

s: Ramakrishna told Narendra that God can only be believed in, never seen
by Narendra's own account, Ramakrishna said yes, he saw God, and could show him too.
Raja Yoga asks readers to believe first and practice later
it asks for no belief at the start: try it, and see what you find.
the poets of the Vedas are called rishis, seers
tradition says the Vedas were seen and heard by them, not made up.

games.q: a classmate says religion just means believing what you're told. by Narendra's story and Vivekananda's Raja Yoga, what's the Hindu answer?
o: agreed: belief comes first, and asking questions is disrespectful.
the sages saw for themselves, and their method invites you to test it.
religion can't be tested, so don't bother trying.
games.why: Narendra asked to see, and Ramakrishna said yes. Vivekananda's Raja Yoga says what one person perceived, others can, and offers the mind as the lab.

practice: Treat this sit as a first experiment: back upright but easy, the breath at its own pace, nothing to reach.
Every few breaths, ask quietly what your mind is doing right now, planning, remembering, listening, drifting, answer honestly with one word, and go back to the breath.
If you pray, you can begin or end with a prayer you already know.

wordCard.voice: Raja Yoga. Vivekananda's book on the yoga of the mind, which asks you to try, and see, before you believe.

orig.note: Sanskrit, in Devanagari: raja yoga, Vivekananda's name for the yoga of the mind.
